hero.intro: Senior frontend engineer moving into systems design and AI. I've built single sign-on for a product family, a web-and-mobile monorepo, a published design system and live audio and video rooms.

intro.label: 01 / Intro
intro.text: Good products are systems. The screen is the part people see; underneath are the shared rules, the sign-in every app trusts and the real-time plumbing that make it feel simple. I've spent three years building both, and now I design the underneath on purpose.

About.metaDescription: The story, experience and toolkit of Toluwalope Akinkunmi, senior frontend engineer moving into systems design and AI.
About.label: About
About.title: A frontend engineer who thinks in systems.

story.p1: I'm Toluwalope Akinkunmi, a senior frontend engineer. For three years I've built web and mobile products end to end, and more and more of my work sits underneath the screens.
story.p2: At The Circular Net I've built most of a product family: the web and mobile apps, an events platform that shares one codebase across web and mobile, the single sign-on every app trusts and a component library published to npm. Alongside that I've worked on payments products at GemsPay, a multilingual trading platform for Hotrac and a CMS for Law x Tech.
story.p3: Now I'm moving into systems design and AI: deciding how the parts fit together, and building products where an LLM does real work. Off-screen I play games, binge series and read.

systems.title: Systems first
systems.body: Before screens, I map the boundaries: what's shared, who owns what, and what happens when a piece fails.

communication.title: Clear communication
communication.body: Short updates, honest timelines and written decisions. You always know what's happening and why.

ownership.title: End-to-end ownership
ownership.body: From the first spec to builds, releases and the bug report after launch, I own the outcome, not just the ticket.

problems.title: Problem solving
problems.body: I dig until I understand the real problem, then pick the simplest thing that solves it.

quality.title: Quality as a habit
quality.body: Every state designed: loading, empty and error. Accessible by default and fast on slow networks.

ai.title: AI where it earns its place
ai.body: I use AI to move faster, and build it into products where it does real work, never as decoration.

the-circular-net-web.title: Social App
the-circular-net-web.summary: The web app of a social network for people and organisations working on sustainability: feed, communities, messaging, live audio and video rooms, jobs, projects and podcasts.
the-circular-net-web.problem: People working on climate and sustainability were scattered across general-purpose networks. The platform needed one place to share, organise, hire and meet, and it had outgrown its first version.
the-circular-net-web.process: I built the first version on the Pages Router in 2023–24, then led the rebuild on the App Router with a module per product area. Chat and live rooms run on Stream and Pusher, posts use a rich-text composer and feeds scroll infinitely. Sign-in moved to a shared SSO service, so every product uses one account.
the-circular-net-web.outcome: Live at app.thecircularnet.com, with deep links into the mobile app. I wrote more than 2,000 commits across the two versions.
the-circular-net-web.learnings: Live rooms are a state machine, not a page. Device setup, screen share and people leaving or being removed all need explicit states, or the interface lies to the user.

built.a: Feed and post composer with media, scheduling, editing, hashtags and saved posts
built.b: Communities, business pages, profiles and a multi-step profile setup
built.c: Direct and group messaging with media previews and rooms attached to chats
built.d: Audio and video rooms with host controls, moderation, raise hand, reactions, screen share and picture-in-picture
built.e: Jobs board, projects hub with milestones, podcasts and events
built.f: Guest pages, link previews and SEO metadata, so shared links work for people without an account

a.title: A module per product area
a.body: Feed, rooms, jobs and the rest each own their routes, components and queries. One area can change without touching the others, and the sprawl of the first version doesn't come back.

b.title: Real-time on managed services
b.body: Stream handles media and chat, and Pusher pushes app events. Building on them let a small team ship live rooms in weeks instead of running media servers.

c.title: Sign-in moved out of the app
c.body: Authentication lives in a separate SSO service, so the web app, Circular Ticket and the marketing site share one account and one secure flow.

the-circular-net-web.system: How the web app fits into the platform

the-circular-net-mobile.title: Social Mobile App
the-circular-net-mobile.tagline: The sustainability network on iOS and Android
the-circular-net-mobile.summary: The iOS and Android app for The Circular Net: feed, communities, messaging, calls, live rooms and podcasts with background playback.
the-circular-net-mobile.problem: The community needed the full platform on their phones, with real-time chat, calls and background audio, not a wrapped website.
the-circular-net-mobile.process: I built the app with Expo and Expo Router, organised by feature module. Rooms and calls run on Stream, chat on a Pusher-backed store, and a podcast player keeps playing in the background. Development, staging and production variants ship through EAS Build and over-the-air updates.
the-circular-net-mobile.outcome: Live on the App Store and Google Play.
the-circular-net-mobile.learnings: Make environments fail loudly. Build variants that refuse to start with the wrong config stopped builds from quietly pointing at the wrong backend.

built.a: Email and Google sign-in, onboarding and a multi-step profile setup
built.b: Feed and post creation with media, scheduling, hashtag autocomplete and full-screen media gestures
built.c: Messaging with document preview and download, plus one-to-one calls with ring detection
built.d: Audio and video rooms with reactions, raise hand, host actions, picture-in-picture and background audio
built.e: A podcast player with mini and full players, queue, resume position and background playback
built.f: Deep links, push notifications, token refresh and an iOS share extension

a.title: Expo over bare React Native
a.body: An earlier bare build was hard to keep moving. Expo, EAS and over-the-air updates let one engineer own builds, releases and fixes.

b.title: Feature modules that mirror the web
b.body: The mobile modules match the web app's areas, so the same mental model, API contracts and naming work on both platforms.

c.title: Three build variants
c.body: Development, staging and production are separate apps with their own config, so testers and real users never share a backend by accident.

the-circular-net-mobile.system: Inside the app and its release pipeline

circular-ticket.title: Circular Ticket
circular-ticket.tagline: Website + web app for events and ticketing
circular-ticket.summary: An events and ticketing product: attendees discover events and buy tickets; organisers create events, scan tickets at the door and get paid in NGN or USD.
circular-ticket.problem: Organisers needed one place to publish events, sell tickets, check people in, verify their identity and get paid. The web and mobile apps were duplicating API calls and business rules, and slowly drifting apart.
circular-ticket.process: I built the web app first, then moved it into an npm-workspaces monorepo with a new Expo app. Services, query hooks, validation schemas and rules like currency formatting and payout eligibility moved into one shared package; screens stayed platform-specific. Each area (events, orders, wallets, payouts, KYC and scanning) was wired to the live API, including Stripe onboarding and bank payouts.
circular-ticket.outcome: The web app is live at circularticket.com. Both apps import the same services and rules, so a change such as when a payout can be requested happens once.
circular-ticket.learnings: Sharing code is a dependency problem before it's a code problem. Aligned versions and careful hoisting across web and native mattered more than the shared code itself.

built.a: Public event pages with SEO metadata, a sitemap and OG images
built.b: A multi-step event wizard with schedules, ticket types, speakers and hybrid venues
built.c: Browser ticket scanning, a scanner hub and staff scanner access
built.d: NGN/USD wallets, transactions, payout accounts and payout requests
built.e: A five-step KYC flow and organiser verification settings
built.f: Orders, registration stats and spreadsheet export for organisers

a.title: Share logic, not screens
a.body: The shared package holds services, hooks, schemas and rules. The interface stays native to each platform, so neither app feels like a port of the other.

b.title: One rule, one place
b.body: Payout eligibility, order status mapping and currency formatting each exist once. Web and mobile can't disagree about money.

c.title: Design every state
c.body: Loading, error, filtered-empty and truly-empty are separate states on every data screen. It made dense organiser dashboards much easier to read.

circular-ticket-mobile.title: Circular Ticket Mobile
circular-ticket-mobile.tagline: The events app for iOS and Android
circular-ticket-mobile.summary: The iOS and Android app for Circular Ticket: attendees discover events and carry their tickets; organisers create events, scan tickets at the door and request payouts.
circular-ticket-mobile.problem: Organisers and attendees needed a native app for the events product, with one account that switches between attendee and organiser roles.
circular-ticket-mobile.process: I built the app in the same npm-workspaces monorepo as the web app, importing services, hooks and schemas from the shared package. It started from mock data and UI primitives, then each area (events, orders, wallets, payouts, KYC and scanning) was wired to the live API.
circular-ticket-mobile.outcome: App identity, deep links and EAS builds for the Play Console are configured; the store release is next.
circular-ticket-mobile.learnings: Sharing data and validation logic kept web and mobile consistent, while the screens stayed native to each platform.

built.a: The attendee flow: discover and filter events, event details, registration, checkout and orders with QR tickets
built.b: The organiser flow: a multi-step create/edit event wizard, dashboard stats, orders and scanner access
built.c: A ticket scanner with camera framing that locks onto the code, validation and attendee check-in
built.d: NGN/USD wallets, transactions, payout accounts and payout requests
built.e: A five-step KYC wizard and in-review states on payout screens
built.f: SSO sign-in, calendar sync, a notifications hub, dark mode and illustrated empty states

a.title: One account, two roles
a.body: Attendees and organisers use the same sign-in and switch roles inside the app, instead of installing two apps.

b.title: Scan, validate, then check in
b.body: The scanner frames the code, validates the ticket against the API and only then checks the attendee in, with a visible state for each step.

c.title: Ready for the newest iOS
c.body: iPad rotation and the iOS scene lifecycle are in from the start, so the app launches cleanly on the latest iOS.

circular-ticket-mobile.system: One app, two roles, the shared package underneath

circular-net-sso.title: Single Sign-On
circular-net-sso.summary: A single sign-on service for The Circular Net's products: login, sign-up and account recovery over OAuth 2.0, with Google and Apple sign-in.
circular-net-sso.problem: Each product had its own login. People needed one account and one secure sign-in across the web app, Circular Ticket and the marketing site.
circular-net-sso.process: I built the OAuth 2.0 authorisation flow with client validation and strict redirect handling, then email and password sign-in with OTP verification, Google and Apple sign-in, and password reset with live strength checks, all as animated multi-step forms with light and dark themes.
circular-net-sso.outcome: Live at accounts.thecircularnet.com as the sign-in entry point for the marketing site, the web app and Circular Ticket.
circular-net-sso.learnings: The SSO page is the one place every app trusts, so it has to be the strictest. Client IDs and redirect URLs are validated, never assumed.

built.a: The OAuth 2.0 authorise flow with client ID validation and redirect handling
built.b: Email and password sign-in and sign-up with OTP email verification
built.c: Google and Apple sign-in with provider callbacks
built.d: Password reset with live strength validation
built.e: Animated multi-step forms, themes and a post-sign-in hand-off page

a.title: A separate app, not a shared component
a.body: Sign-in runs on its own domain. Apps redirect to it and get a code back, so no product ever handles another product's passwords.

b.title: Strict redirects
b.body: Only registered clients and redirect URLs are accepted. An open redirect on a sign-in page is a ready-made phishing kit.

c.title: React 19 and the React Compiler
c.body: The forms are animation-heavy. The compiler keeps re-renders in check without hand-written memoisation.

circular-net-sso.system: Every product signs in through one service

circular-net-website.title: Website
circular-net-website.summary: The public site for The Circular Net: the platform, its sustainability services and a blog, with sign-in that hands people over to the app.
circular-net-website.problem: The company needed a site that explains the product and its services, ranks in search and routes visitors into the apps.
circular-net-website.process: I built the home and service pages as feature modules with motion and smooth scrolling, then a blog with a password-gated publishing page. A later pass covered SEO, web vitals and accessibility, plus redirects for old indexed links.
circular-net-website.outcome: Live at thecircularnet.com, showing upcoming events from the API and handing signed-in users over to the web app.
circular-net-website.learnings: Server-side secrets behave differently on every host. The blog admin needed specific handling for the hosting platform's server rendering.

built.a: The home page with feature showcases and live upcoming events
built.b: Carbon Accounting, ESG Reporting and Sustainability Projects pages
built.c: A blog with article pages, a white-paper download and sharing
built.d: A password-gated page for publishing posts
built.e: An SEO overhaul: metadata, sitemap, generated OG images, redirects and accessibility fixes

a.title: Sign-in through SSO, with a state check
a.body: The site starts the SSO flow with a state value it checks on return, so a forged callback can't sign someone in.

b.title: Redirect old links instead of losing them
b.body: The old site's indexed URLs map to the new pages, keeping search traffic through the relaunch.

export-trades.title: Export Trades
export-trades.tagline: Cross-border commodity trading, in many languages
export-trades.summary: A marketing site and trading web app that connects commodity buyers and sellers and walks them through quotes, offers, escrow and delivery.
export-trades.problem: Commodity buyers and sellers needed a trusted place to find products, negotiate and complete trades across borders and across languages, including right-to-left Arabic.
export-trades.process: I built the public site (marketplace, commodities and market trends) and the signed-in app around one module per trading step. Locale-based routing and translations went in from the start, and verification documents upload straight to storage.
export-trades.outcome: Live at exportrades.com. Version 0.9 of the site and app shipped in February 2026; I was the largest contributor on a five-person team.
export-trades.learnings: Build translation in from day one. Adding a right-to-left language later would have meant touching every layout.

built.a: The public site: marketplace, commodity categories, market index and trends
built.b: Sign-up with country selection and OTP, login and profile editing
built.c: Product pages with specifications, certificates and FAQs
built.d: Requests for quote, expressions of interest, offers and trades, with user and admin views
built.e: Escrow setup, dispute management and transaction history

a.title: A module per trading step
a.body: Quotes, offers, trades, escrow and disputes are separate modules with their own data and views, mirroring how a deal actually moves.

b.title: Locale in the URL
b.body: Every page lives under its locale, so links, search engines and right-to-left layouts all know the language without guessing.

c.title: Shared views, separate permissions
c.body: Users and admins see the same trade records through different views, instead of two copies of the logic.

lawxtech.title: Law x Tech
lawxtech.tagline: A home for Africa's law and technology community
lawxtech.summary: The website and CMS of Law x Tech, a 2,000+ member community at the intersection of law and technology that runs series, a summit and awards.
lawxtech.problem: The organisation needed a modern site it could update itself. On the original site, every new episode or partner meant asking a developer.
lawxtech.process: I built the first site in React in 2023. In 2026 I rebuilt it on Next.js 16 with motion, then added an admin CMS backed by Postgres: credential sign-in, a rich-text blog editor, image uploads and role-based user management. Larger features, like partners, started as a written spec and plan before any code.
lawxtech.outcome: Live at lawxtech.org, with the team publishing content themselves.
lawxtech.learnings: Serverless databases need care around connection pooling and build-time access. The build should never depend on the database being reachable.

built.a: A home page with animated stats, series preview, speakers carousel and community sections
built.b: About, Series, Summit & Awards, Careers, Contact and Sponsors pages
built.c: Partners with detail pages and a summit countdown
built.d: An admin CMS with a rich-text editor and image uploads
built.e: User management with roles and admin-only access

a.title: A CMS instead of content in code
a.body: The first site kept content in code and the team couldn't update it. The redesign gives them an editor, so the site stays current without me.

b.title: Postgres and blob storage, not a hosted CMS
b.body: Neon Postgres and Vercel Blob keep running costs near zero for a volunteer-run organisation, with no per-seat fees.

c.title: Spec before code
c.body: Bigger features were written up as a design spec and plan first, which made the scope clear to non-technical organisers.

lawxtech.system: Public site and CMS on one database

pennywise.title: Pennywise
pennywise.summary: A personal-finance mobile app for tracking spending, budgets and goals, plus the marketing site that collected its waitlist.
pennywise.problem: People wanted to see where their money goes and stick to budgets from their phone, and the product needed a site to explain itself and collect sign-ups before launch.
pennywise.process: I built the app with Expo and Expo Router: onboarding, sign-up with verification, password reset, wallets, budgets and charts, with bank account linking through a third-party widget. The website started on the Pages Router with Mantine and was later rebuilt on the App Router with Tailwind.
pennywise.outcome: Both versions of the website are live, and the app ships through separate staging and preview build channels.
pennywise.learnings: Android builds and network configuration take real time. Budget for platform work alongside feature work.

built.a: Onboarding, sign-up, verification and a multi-step password reset
built.b: Wallets and budgets with charts drawn in Skia
built.c: Bank account linking and secure local storage
built.d: EAS build channels for staging and preview
built.e: A landing site with waitlist, pricing, community and blog pages

a.title: Fast local storage
a.body: MMKV keeps settings and session data on the device, so the app opens straight into the right state.

b.title: From a component library to Tailwind
b.body: The second version of the site dropped the component library for Tailwind, which made theming and later changes much simpler.

invocipt.title: Invocipt
invocipt.tagline: Invoices, payments and receipts for small businesses
invocipt.summary: A SaaS platform where businesses create invoices, get paid online and turn paid invoices into receipts, with several businesses per account, product catalogues and customer records.
invocipt.problem: Small businesses juggle invoices in documents, payments in banking apps and receipts on paper, with no single record of who paid for what.
invocipt.process: I built it as a full-stack Next.js app on Postgres with Prisma. One account can run several businesses, each with its own products (importable from a spreadsheet), customers, bank details and payment integrations. Every invoice gets a public page with a QR code where the customer pays through Paystack or Flutterwave, and a paid invoice becomes a receipt in one click. Emails go out through Resend with React Email templates, and the installable web app sends push notifications.
invocipt.outcome: Version 1.0 shipped in February 2025, followed by regular releases through June 2025 with an automated public changelog.
invocipt.learnings: Money flows need explicit states. Draft, unpaid and paid invoices behave differently, and modelling that up front kept payments, emails and reports consistent.

built.a: Multi-business workspaces with products, customers, bank details and team roles
built.c: Invoices with drafts, QR codes and a public payment page (Paystack, Flutterwave)
built.d: One-click receipts from paid invoices, with PDF download
built.e: Email notifications with React Email templates and web push notifications
built.f: A revenue dashboard, reports, an admin area, a blog and a public changelog

a.title: Payments go to the business
a.body: Each business connects its own payment gateway keys, so customers pay the business directly and Invocipt never holds the money.

b.title: Invoice status drives everything
b.body: Draft, unpaid and paid are explicit statuses, and emails, dashboards and receipts all follow them instead of guessing.

c.title: Release discipline, even solo
c.body: Conventional commits, commit linting, Git hooks and automated releases keep version numbers and the public changelog in step.

invocipt.system: From invoice to payment to receipt

life-fount.title: Life Fount
life-fount.tagline: A multilingual website for a medical centre
life-fount.summary: The website of Life Fount Medical Center: 18 services with their own pages, in English, Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa, built mobile-first for patients on their phones.
life-fount.problem: Patients look a hospital up on their phone, often in a language other than English, and want to know quickly what it treats and how to reach someone.
life-fount.process: I built the site on Next.js with next-intl, so every page exists in English, Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa under its own URL. Each of the 18 services, from cardiology to physiotherapy, gets a page generated from one data file. The layout is mobile-first with motion throughout, plus a floating WhatsApp button for quick questions, FAQs, testimonials, careers and a contact form.
life-fount.learnings: Designing for four languages means layouts that flex with the length of the text, instead of being tuned to English.

built.a: A home page with hero, services, why-choose-us, stats, testimonials and FAQs
built.b: 18 service pages generated from a single data file
built.c: English, Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa, with a language switcher and localised URLs
built.d: A floating WhatsApp button for quick patient questions
built.e: About, careers and contact pages with a validated contact form
built.f: SEO metadata, a sitemap, a web app manifest and light and dark themes

a.title: Nigerian languages, first-class
a.body: Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa get their own routes instead of a machine-translation widget, so every page can be shared and found in the patient's language.

b.title: Services as data
b.body: All 18 services live in one data file, so adding or updating a department is a content change, not a new page.

c.title: WhatsApp over a chat widget
c.body: Patients already use WhatsApp, so the support button opens a conversation there instead of an embedded chat that needs its own staff.

architekt.title: Architekt
architekt.tagline: An agency website with an AI pricing advisor
architekt.summary: The website of a digital agency for websites, web apps and mobile apps, with a project portfolio, a pricing calculator and a questionnaire where an LLM recommends a plan, add-ons and a cost estimate.
architekt.problem: People want a ballpark price before they talk to an agency, but fixed price lists don't fit custom work, and a long sales call is a big ask for a small client.
architekt.process: I designed and built the site on Next.js with motion throughout: services, how-we-work, featured projects, testimonials, careers and a contact page with a Mapbox map. Pricing combines fixed tiers, add-ons and an interactive calculator. A short questionnaire sends the project type, complexity, features, timeline and budget to Gemini through Genkit, which returns a recommended tier, add-ons and an estimate as structured data. Resend then emails the result to both the visitor and the agency.
architekt.outcome: In progress. The site and the AI questionnaire run on a preview deployment while the remaining pages are finished.
architekt.learnings: Constrain the model's output. A strict schema for tier, add-ons and cost turned the AI's answer into data the interface and emails could use directly, instead of free text.

built.a: A home page with services, how-we-work, featured projects, testimonials and client logos
built.b: A project portfolio with detail pages and a similar-projects carousel
built.c: Pricing tiers, add-ons and an interactive pricing calculator
built.d: An AI pricing questionnaire using Gemini 2.5 Flash through Genkit
built.e: Confirmation and lead emails through Resend
built.f: About, careers and contact pages with a Mapbox map, plus light and dark themes

a.title: Structured output, not chat
a.body: The model returns a typed object (tier, add-ons, cost) checked against a schema, so the result renders as a proper recommendation, not a paragraph.

b.title: Real prices in the prompt
b.body: The tiers and add-on prices are given to the model explicitly, so estimates stay within the agency's actual price list instead of being invented.

c.title: Every answer becomes a lead
c.body: The recommendation is emailed to both the visitor and the agency, so the first conversation starts with scope and budget already on the table.

architekt.system: From questionnaire to recommendation to lead

stock-bot.title: Stock Bot
stock-bot.tagline: An AI analyst for the Nigerian stock market
stock-bot.summary: A scheduled agent that scans the Nigerian Exchange every day, checks recent price history, asks an LLM to assess each dip and sends me a short report on Telegram.
stock-bot.problem: Finding good dips on the NGX means checking dozens of stocks every day and reading the story behind each drop. I wanted the boring part automated and the judgement call summarised.
stock-bot.process: A Lambda function runs on a daily EventBridge schedule. It scrapes the day's biggest losers, so only those get a closer look, compares them with five days of prices stored in DynamoDB and sends the candidates to Gemini for a short analysis. The top picks arrive on Telegram, and GitHub Actions deploys every push.
stock-bot.outcome: In progress. Scraping, analysis and Telegram reports work locally; the Lambda deployment is being finalised.
stock-bot.learnings: Filter before you spend tokens or requests. Starting from the day's losers instead of every ticker cut the work to a fraction.

built.a: A parallel scraper for the NGX daily losers
built.b: Five days of price history in DynamoDB to confirm a real dip
built.c: An LLM analysis step with a structured prompt per company
built.d: Daily Telegram reports with the top picks
built.e: Continuous deployment to AWS Lambda with GitHub Actions

a.title: Serverless on a schedule
a.body: The job runs for a couple of minutes a day. A scheduled Lambda costs almost nothing and needs no server to look after.

b.title: Filter first, then think
b.body: Cheap code narrows the list, and the LLM only sees the few stocks worth a closer look. It keeps both latency and cost down.

c.title: Drop heavy dependencies
c.body: Replacing pandas with a lightweight HTML parser made the Lambda package small enough to deploy without special layers.

stock-bot.system: A daily run, from schedule to report

trendhub.title: TrendHub
trendhub.tagline: A hub for newsletters, podcasts and blogs
trendhub.summary: One place for Gen Z readers to explore newsletters, podcasts and blogs and keep up with what's trending.
trendhub.problem: Good writing is scattered across newsletters, podcasts and blogs. I wanted one light, welcoming place to find it.
trendhub.process: I built it on Next.js 13 with TypeScript and Redux Toolkit, with motion to keep browsing playful and a minimal, dark-mode-friendly reading view.
trendhub.outcome: Live, with more than 100 active readers.
trendhub.learnings: Minimal design is a lot of decisions. Every option I removed made reading easier.

coinsave.title: Coinsave
coinsave.summary: Take control of your finances: track income and expenses, set budgets, get notified, and monitor bank transactions in one place.
coinsave.problem: Most people know they should budget but drop off after a week. Spreadsheets are tedious and banking apps only show what already happened.
coinsave.process: I designed a fast, low-friction flow for logging spending, built budgets with smart alerts, and connected bank transaction monitoring so the app does most of the work.
coinsave.outcome: Coinsave grew to more than 500 active users with over 70% engagement and an average rating of 4.5 out of 5.
coinsave.learnings: Retention is a product feature. Small touches like sensible defaults and timely nudges mattered more than any big feature.

cabify.title: Cabify
cabify.summary: Hassle-free travel with easy booking, real-time updates and secure payments for rides in buses and cabs.
cabify.problem: Booking a ride meant juggling calls, cash and uncertainty about when the driver would actually show up.
cabify.process: I built the booking and tracking interfaces with a focus on performance, so the app loads fast and navigation feels smooth even on slow connections.
cabify.outcome: More than 500 active users, over 70% engagement and an average rating of 4.5 out of 5.
cabify.learnings: Perceived speed is real speed. Skeletons, optimistic updates and fewer round-trips changed how fast the app felt.
